query: Consider the following context: High-temperature self-lubricating materials with stable tribological performance across a wide temperature range are essential for advanced mechanical systems under extreme conditions. However, balancing mechanical strength and lubrication efficiency remains a key challenge. In that context, which material can be used for high-performance wide-temperature self-lubricating materials, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Applying a multilayer or functionally graded surface coating to a nanocrystalline CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy film will foster in situ formation of a stable lubricious tribofilm at elevated temperatures, thereby extending its self-lubricating performance over a wider temperature range without sacrificing mechanical strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanocrystalline CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy film prepared via single-target magnetron sputtering.
generation.intervention: Introduce a multilayer or functionally graded coating on the RHEA film, designed to tailor the top interface so that controlled oxidation or nitride formation occurs during operation.
generation.conditions: High-temperature operating conditions from room temperature up to at least 300 °C, with potential extension to higher temperatures under extreme load and thermal cycling.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an adaptive, stable lubricious surface tribofilm (such as an oxide or nitride layer) that remains bound to the underlying high-strength alloy.
generation.mechanism: The engineered surface layer, through its gradual compositional and structural variation, promotes the in situ development of a tribofilm that reduces friction while preserving the mechanical integrity of the underlying RHEA during high-temperature exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: The multilayer-coated alloy will exhibit a lower friction coefficient and enhanced wear resistance across the extended temperature range compared to the unmodified film, while maintaining its high hardness and strength.
generation.baseline: The unmodified nanocrystalline CuMoTaWV film, which has demonstrated effective performance up to 300 °C but shows limitations in self-lubrication and wear resistance at higher temperatures.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are contingent on the stability of the tribofilm and coating structure; performance might decline if the interface layer degrades at extremely high temperatures or under long-term cyclic thermal loads.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature range over which the tribofilm remains effective and the long-term durability of the multilayer coating under cyclic extreme conditions require further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the nanocrystalline CuMoTaWV films with the engineered multilayer (functionally graded) surface coating, and an identical set without the coating. Subject both sets to standardized high-temperature tribological testing across a temperature range from room temperature to 600 °C under identical applied loads and sliding conditions.
measurements: Measure friction coefficient at various temperatures using a tribometer.
Quantify wear rate and material loss through mass change or profilometry.
Characterize surface morphology and composition of the tribofilm using SEM/EDS.
Assess any changes in hardness and overall mechanical strength using microhardness testing.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the multilayer-coated samples fail to show a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the unmodified samples over the tested temperature range, or if the coating degrades prematurely resulting in diminished mechanical properties.

Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In this study, the wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy coating was systematically analyzed by the molecular dynamics method. FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy was used as a coating material to adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix. The friction and nanoindentation simulation of this coating material were carried out by controlling the ambient temperature. The influence of temperature on its friction properties was analyzed on five aspects: lattice structure, dislocation evolution, friction coefficient, hardness, and elastic modulus. The results show that with the increase of temperature, the disorder of the lattice structure increases, which leads to an increase of the tangential force and friction coefficient in the friction process. decision.trend: In 2020, researchers investigated a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (CuMoTaWV) film deposited by single-target magnetron sputtering for improved tribological performance. They demonstrated high hardness and enhanced wear resistance, with annealing further boosting adhesion and reducing friction at room temperature and 300 °C. However, achieving stable and efficient self-lubrication over a broader temperature range—especially at higher temperatures—remains a challenge, as the tested film’s friction data are primarily limited to 300 °C. Extending lubricative properties beyond this range without sacrificing the alloy’s mechanical benefits is still unresolved.
decision.unsolved: Ensuring reliable lubrication and wear protection across a significantly wider temperature range—up to very high temperatures—while maintaining mechanical strength is an open problem not yet addressed by current coatings. The core difficulty lies in sustaining a lubricious surface film under more extreme conditions without altering the alloy composition.
decision.lever: Adopt a multilayer or functionally graded coating approach to form a stable lubricious top layer that adapts to temperature changes and wear conditions, leveraging the existing CuMoTaWV film’s high hardness and strength. This could involve tailoring the topmost interface to create in situ tribofilms (e.g., oxide or nitride layers) while preserving the underlying RHEA’s mechanical integrity.
decision.why: Shifting to a carefully engineered surface or interface design avoids compositional changes while enabling a stable, self-lubricating layer to form at higher temperatures. This aligns with the successful tribological results at 300 °C and directly addresses the need to maintain lubrication efficiency and mechanical robustness over an extended temperature range.
